name: Arko Art Center
funding: State-run: operated by Arts Council Korea.
watch: State-funded. Parent Arts Council Korea gave grant juries a political blacklist of artists in 2015, exposed in a National Assembly inspection.
records_note: No records of its own; parent Arts Council Korea posts reports 2019 to 2025, lists its council and files accounts on ALIO.
affiliations_note: Run by Arts Council Korea, which also runs the Arko and Daehangno Arts Theatre, Arko Arts Archive, Artists' House and a training institute. Member of CIMAM.

overview: Public art museum in the Daehakro district of Seoul, in Marronnier Park on the former site of Seoul National University, next to ARKO Arts Theater (CIMAM).
Began in 1974 as Misulhoegwan. Moved to its present building in 1979, began curating its own exhibitions in the 1990s, was renamed Marronnier Art Center in 2002 and Arko Art Center in 2005 (CIMAM).
Named for Arts Council Korea (ARKO), the body that runs it (CIMAM; Arts Council Korea).
Building: brick, designed by the architect Kim Swoo-geun (CIMAM). The Korea Times (Cathy Rose A. Garcia, 26 May 2009) mentions the centre's red bricks.
Programmes: thematic exhibitions on social subjects and public programmes. Insa Art Space, opened in 2000, and the IAS Studio programme (CIMAM).
Visiting: open Tuesday to Sunday, 11:00 to 19:00 (last entry 18:30), until 21:00 on Wednesdays. Closed Mondays, 1 January, Seollal and Chuseok. Admission is free (centre website).
details.funding_verdict: Arko Art Center: state-run: operated by Arts Council Korea
funding: Arts Council Korea was established in 1973 and lists the Arko Art Center among its platforms (Arts Council Korea).
ArtReview (Hyunjin Kim, 12 Aug 2016) places Arts Council Korea among art and culture funding organisations with "a very strong affiliation with the Ministry" of Culture, Sports and Tourism.

press.overall: One opinion piece criticises the parent body, Arts Council Korea, not the centre.

items.title: Hyunjin Kim, "Self-censored" (12 Aug 2016)
points: Argues that censorship in South Korea has moved from removing artworks after the fact to preventive measures through funding and personnel decisions, "designed to eradicate controversial elements in advance".
Argues that artists and curators who choose compromise over resistance leave bureaucrats free to manage and control artists.

Names Arts Council Korea (ARKO) as under scrutiny, and says a blacklist of artists, directors and writers was given to funding juries in theatre and literature, revealed after media coverage and a National Assembly inspection of ARKO. Does not name the Arko Art Center.

wider_context: The Korea Times (Choi Ha-young, 12 Oct 2016): opposition lawmaker Do Jong-hwan cited minutes of a 29 May 2015 Arts Council Korea meeting at a National Assembly audit. Kwon Young-bin, then head of Arts Council Korea, is quoted saying "we can't make decisions on our own".

Unverified: Hankook Ilbo reported, via The Korea Herald (Yeo Jun-suk, 13 Oct 2016), that a 100-page document listed 9,473 artists and that the presidential office told government agencies, including Arts Council Korea, to cut support to entities linked to them. Cheong Wa Dae and the government denied it, and Culture Minister Cho Yoon-sun told lawmakers there was no such blacklist.

Yonhap, via The Korea Times (23 Jan 2018): the Seoul High Court raised former presidential chief of staff Kim Ki-choon's sentence to four years and gave former culture minister Cho Yoon-sun two years in prison, ruling that the government's exclusion of critical artists from state support violated the Constitution. The report names neither Arts Council Korea nor the Arko Art Center.
Arts Council Korea operates the Arko Art Center (centre website); the juries named in ArtReview were in theatre and literature.
details.bottom_line: The money behind the centre is public and comes through Arts Council Korea. The 2015 to 2016 artist blacklist is tied in the sources to the parent body and its funding juries in theatre and literature, and the 2018 court findings concerned the presidential chief of staff and the culture minister. Worth watching is how the parent body awards support, since the centre sits inside it.

name: Art Sonje Center
watch: Private non-profit contemporary kunsthalle in Seoul founded by Chung Hee-ja.
records_note: It links the Daewoo Foundation and invites corporate sponsors only.
affiliations_note: Its parent is the Art Sonje Museum in Gyeongju, founded in 1991 by the same founder.

overview: Private contemporary art centre at 87 Yulgok-ro 3-gil, Jongno-gu, Seoul (the centre's own site). Wikipedia places it in Samcheong-dong.

Founded and chaired by Heeja K. Chung (Chung Hee-ja), whom the centre's site calls "a pioneering female business leader and a distinguished patron of the arts and culture in Korea". Opened in 1998. It grew out of the "Sprout" exhibition programme held in 1995 in a hanok house and a Western-style house on the site.
The centre says Chung founded it to honour her love of art and to remember her late son, Kim Son-je. The centre's site says Chung also founded the Sonje Museum of Art in Gyeongju in 1991.
Building: three floors and a basement on a street corner that was previously a traditional hanok home, designed by the architect Kim Jong-sung (the centre's facilities page).

On site: exhibition spaces of 174 to 466 square metres, a learning space, a 238-seat basement Art Hall with a proscenium stage and a digital cinema projector, an inner hanok-style garden and a rooftop garden. The centre's programme covers exhibitions, screenings, performances, publications, new productions and research.
Open Tuesday to Sunday, 12:00 to 18:00. Closed Monday. Tickets are sold through a Naver booking page.
details.funding_verdict: Art Sonje Center: private non-profit, stated by the centre to be an extension of the Daewoo Foundation's arts work
funding: The centre states that it was founded as an extension of the Daewoo Foundation's social-sharing work in the arts (artsonje.org, About).

The Daewoo Foundation page on artsonje.org says the foundation's projects "have been primarily funded by the late Daewoo Group chairperson Kim Woo Choong since 1978". Chung married Kim in 1964; he died in 2019 (artsonje.org, Founder page).
not_related: the Wooyang Museum of Art in Gyeongju. It was the Art Sonje Museum, run by Daewoo Development; Wooyang Industrial Development bought Daewoo Development at auction in 2012 and renamed it. The Seoul centre kept the Art Sonje name (USA Art News). Chung sought the return of 188 artworks from Wooyang; the court ordered three of them returned to her (USA Art News).

press.overall: One review praises a show at the centre and has one reservation about it.

items.title: Ian Tee, "Editor's Notes: Exhibitions in Seoul" (2026)
points: Praises "Spectrosynthesis Seoul" at the centre as an "unapologetically queer" show and credits the curators for including many Korean artists.
Says the show needed "more breathing room" for the nuances among works and contexts to come through.
Criticises the show, not the institution.

wider_context: Kim Woo-choong, founder and former chairman of Daewoo, was sentenced on 30 May 2006 by the Seoul Central District Court to 10 years in prison, forfeiture of more than 21 trillion won and a fine of 10 million won. The court found accounting fraud of over 20 trillion won, 9.8 trillion won of illegal financing, 19 trillion won diverted abroad and $100 million embezzled (AP via NBC News).
Daewoo collapsed under massive debts in the wake of the 1997 to 1998 Asian financial crisis (AP via NBC News).

The centre says it was founded as an extension of the Daewoo Foundation's commitment to social sharing practices in the arts, and the foundation's page on the centre's site says its projects have been primarily funded by Kim since 1978. Chung, the centre's founder, married Kim in 1964.
details.bottom_line: The centre is a family-founded private non-profit that says it was founded as an extension of the Daewoo Foundation's arts work; the foundation says Kim Woo-choong primarily funded its projects from 1978. Kim was convicted of fraud and embezzlement in 2006, a case that belongs to the founder personally.

name: Busan Museum of Contemporary Art
funding: Municipal museum on Eulsukdo, run by Busan Metropolitan City; it hosted part of the 2026 Busan Biennale.
watch: Only the building and garden have drawn criticism.
records_note: It only shows an organisation chart and the governing ordinance.
affiliations_note: The city's second municipal art museum after Busan Museum of Art, and a venue of the 2026 Busan Biennale. Member of Gallery Climate Coalition.

overview: Public contemporary art museum at 1191 Nakdongnam-ro, Saha-gu, on Eulsukdo island, which KNN describes as a bird migration site.

Construction began in November 2013 and finished in February 2017. The museum opened officially on 15 June 2018 and was registered as a Type 1 museum in May 2018 (museum site). Its origins go back to a 2005 study for a dedicated Busan Biennale space and a 2009 basic plan for a second municipal museum.
Kim Seongyoun became first director on 11 May 2017 and Kang Seungwan second director on 27 June 2022 (museum site).
The exterior carries a "Vertical Garden" by Patrick Blanc with 175 plant species native to Korea, and the children's art library was designed by the architect Lee Ki-chul (Newsis, 27 May 2018).

The museum focuses on contemporary art including new media art, with attention to nature and ecosystems (stated by the museum). It was a venue of the 2018 Busan Biennale (Wikipedia) and hosts the first part of the 2026 edition (e-flux).

Open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00. Closed Mondays and 1 January. Admission is free except for special exhibitions (museum site). The Busan Biennale 2026 exhibition at the museum charges 16,000 won for adults (Busan Metropolitan City).
details.funding_verdict: Busan Museum of Contemporary Art: public: Busan city government
funding: The museum describes itself as a public art museum and sits on the Busan city government's website; the Busan city government announced its 2018 opening (Newsis).
A proposed rooftop restaurant would use nearly 2 billion won in city funds (KNN, 16 September 2024).

press.overall: One local news report, from 2024, covers objections to a proposed rooftop restaurant; it is not art-press criticism of the programme.

items.title: Hwangbo Ram, "부산현대미술관 옥상에 음식점 추진 논란" (16 September 2024; my translation: Controversy over a plan for a restaurant on the Busan Museum of Contemporary Art rooftop)
points: Reports that the museum wants a rooftop restaurant seating about 60, open at night, on the building that houses the art storage; an art-sector source said major museums typically keep restaurants away from storage areas, and the report notes fire concerns.

Park Sang-hyeon of the Busan Environmental Movement Association warned that birds are highly sensitive to light and that night operations could disrupt their migration routes on Eulsukdo, which the report calls a protected heritage zone; Song Sang-jo, chair of the city council's administration and culture committee, said operating costs and hours need scrutiny.
The museum said it would install special glass to limit light pollution and make supplementary design changes for safety.

details.bottom_line: The museum is a public art museum of the Busan city government. The one documented dispute is the 2024 rooftop restaurant plan, which an environmental group and a city councillor questioned over bird habitat and operating costs, and an art-sector source over fire safety near the art store.

name: Nam June Paik Art Center
funding: Hyundai Motor supports the Hyundai Translocal Series, announced in February 2025, in which the center exchanges with the Pinacoteca de São Paulo.
watch: Reuters reported in July 2022 that SMART, a Hyundai subsidiary in Alabama, hired minors as young as 12.
why_flagged: The flag rests on Hyundai Motor, which supports the Hyundai Translocal Series with the center.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: Its parent foundation posts yearbooks for 2012 to 2025, settlement papers and a named board; the centre shows sponsor logos only, undated.
affiliations_note: Run by the Gyeonggi Cultural Foundation, which also runs the Gyeonggi Museum of Modern Art, Gyeonggi Museum, Silhak Museum, Jeongok Prehistory Museum and children's museums.

overview: Public art centre in Giheung-gu, Yongin, Gyeonggi Province, at 10 Paiknamjune-ro (Gyeonggi Province English site). Wikipedia names Giheung station as the nearest transit.

The basic plan was set with the artist Nam June Paik in November 2001. The building opened with a Nam June Paik Festival on 8 October 2008 (Gyeonggi Province English site). Paik died before he saw it (JoongAng Daily, Chung Jae-sook, 7 April 2010).
Named for Nam June Paik, the Korean American video artist. Its permanent collection is of his work, with temporary exhibitions (Wikipedia).

Designed by Kirsten Schemel and Marina Stankovic of KSMS Schemel Stankovic Architects, Berlin, who won a 2003 international competition of 430 entries (centre site). Three storeys above ground and two below, about 5,600 square metres on a 30,983 square metre site, with a screen facade of layered reflective and partly printed glass.
Holds galleries, a video archive and multi-purpose spaces (centre site). It awards the Nam June Paik Art Center Prize, first given in 2009 (Wikipedia).

Visiting: Tuesday to Sunday 10am to 6pm (until 7pm in July and August), closed Mondays, 1 January and Thanksgiving. Adults 4,000 won. Students and soldiers 2,000 won. Under 6, over 66 and people with disabilities free (Gyeonggi Province English site, undated). The centre's own site lists sign language interpretation for exhibition guides. The Gyeonggi page shows a 25% discount for Gyeonggi Province residents and a 50% discount for adult groups of 20 or more.
details.funding_verdict: Nam June Paik Art Center: public: Gyeonggi Province through the Gyeonggi Cultural Foundation, with support from Hyundai Motor for its exhibitions
funding: The centre is run by the Gyeonggi Cultural Foundation (centre site footer). The site states that individual donations and corporate and organisational sponsorship support its programmes.

Hyundai Motor money reaching the centre today: Hyundai Motor Group (23 June 2026) says it runs the Hyundai Translocal Series, launched in 2025, in which the centre and the Pinacoteca de Sao Paulo co-organise an exhibition opening in November 2026; the Herald (22 June 2026) describes Hyundai Motor as the series' organiser and does not say Hyundai sponsors the centre directly. The Gyeonggi Ilbo (June 2025) reports that the 2025 programme was set at four exhibitions "thanks to Hyundai Motor's sponsorship" (translation from the Korean), against an exhibition budget of 510 million won.

red_flags.heading: Hyundai and child labour at a subsidiary
points: July 2022: Reuters reported that SMART, a Hyundai subsidiary in Luverne, Alabama, hired minors as young as 12; a former employee estimated about 50 (Wikipedia, summarising Reuters). SMART supplies parts to Hyundai's Montgomery plant. Hyundai said it does not tolerate illegal employment practices at any Hyundai entity.

Authorities: after an inspection on 9 August 2022, the US Department of Labor fined SL Alabama, another supplier, $30,076 on 29 September 2022 and a federal consent decree barred it from shipping goods made with underage labour. The Alabama Department of Labor fined SL Alabama and JK USA $17,800 each. Neither agency accused Hyundai or Kia of wrongdoing, and the article reports no fine against SMART itself (Wikipedia).
24 February 2023: Hyundai CEO Jae Hoon Chang told shareholders Hyundai would divest its controlling stake in SMART (Wikipedia).
Link to the centre: Hyundai Motor's support for the centre is described under FUNDING; no source opened connects the Alabama case to the centre.

details.bottom_line: The money is mainly Gyeonggi Province's public budget, with support from Hyundai Motor for its exhibitions. The weak points are the undisclosed size and term of the Hyundai support and Hyundai's 2022 child-labour case at its Alabama subsidiary, whose controlling stake it said in February 2023 it would divest. Worth watching: whether the foundation publishes sponsor amounts for the Translocal Series.

name: National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA)
funding: State museum. Hyundai Motor sponsored its series from 2014 to February 2024; LG Electronics sponsors the OLED Series from 2025. The Lee Kun-hee estate gave nearly 1,500 works in 2021.
watch: Hyundai Motor sponsored its series to February 2024. Reuters found children as young as 12 at Hyundai subsidiary SMART Alabama in 2022.
tier_note: No reason for the flag is recorded.
records_note: Its sponsorship page points to a separate foundation site.
affiliations_note: Runs four venues: Seoul, Gwacheon, Deoksugung and Cheongju. The pages read name no network, university or partner museum. Member of CIMAM, Res Artis.

overview: South Korea's national museum of modern and contemporary Korean art, with four sites: Gwacheon, Deoksugung, Seoul (next to Gyeongbokgung) and Cheongju (a storage and conservation centre) (Wikipedia).
Established in 1969. It first opened in Gyeongbokgung on 20 October 1969, moved to Deoksugung in 1973 and to Gwacheon in 1986. The Seoul site opened on 13 November 2013 (Wikipedia).
It is a state museum under the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, which removed one director in 2014 and accepted another's resignation in 2023 (Korea JoongAng Daily; ArtReview).
details.funding_verdict: National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA): state museum under the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, with corporate series sponsors
funding: Hyundai Motor sponsored one solo exhibition of a mid-career Korean artist each year from 2014: 12 billion won over 10 years, announced in November 2013 and the largest sponsorship in the museum's history; the tenth and final show ran through 25 February 2024 (Hankyung Magazine, Lee Seung-ryul, 18 September 2023, translated).
LG Electronics is title sponsor of the MMCA x LG OLED Series, a multi-year partnership whose first exhibition, TZUSOO, ran from 1 August 2025 to 1 February 2026 (LG newsroom, 31 July 2025).

red_flags.heading: Protest against the director's appointment (2015)
points: In November 2015 the Korean campaign group petition4art launched a petition against the candidacy of Bartomeu Marí as MMCA director over his handling of an exhibition at Macba in Barcelona. More than 830 Korean artists, curators and cultural figures signed it (The Art Newspaper, Gareth Harris, 8 December 2015).

A second petition, launched on 3 December 2015 and signed by 450 people by the article's date, was aimed at the Ministry of Culture; a petition4art spokesperson said the ministry must not attempt any kind of censorship and asked the new director for a public declaration against censorship. Marí was appointed in early December 2015 (The Art Newspaper).

red_flags.heading: State censorship at the opening show (2013)
points: Unverified: six politically awkward works were dropped from the opening show Zeitgeist Korea less than a week before opening, and the Blue House had a hand in the final selection, from the Korea Times as relayed by Philip Gowman on the blog London Korean Links (28 November 2013); the post names no individual source.

press.overall: Criticism concerns appointments, nepotism and political pressure on the state museum.

items.title: Gareth Harris, "Korean artists protest appointment of former Barcelona museum director due to censorship concerns" (8 December 2015)
points: Reports two petitions started by petition4art against Marí, who cancelled the Macba exhibition The Beast and the Sovereign (including a work by Ines Doujak) on the eve of its launch, reopened it on 21 March 2015 and resigned that month.
Marí says he opposes "all sorts of censorship" and defends his Macba decision.

items.title: "Director of South Korea's MMCA museums steps down amid alleged political pressure" (21 April 2023)
points: Youn Bum-mo, director from 2019 and reappointed in 2022, resigned; Korean media speculated about political pressure after the March 2022 presidential election, and the article says the exact cause is unclear.

A ministry audit listed 16 allegations of illegal or inappropriate practices, including questionable auction acquisitions and failure to address workplace bullying; critics alleged nepotism in his reappointment.

items.title: Moon So-young, "MMCA chief dismissed in recruitment controversy" (22 October 2014)
points: The ministry dismissed director Chung Hyung-min after the Board of Audit and Inspection found evidence that she intervened in an October 2013 curator recruitment; the board asked prosecutors to investigate her for "abuse of authority".

wider_context: Wikipedia (Hyundai Alabama child labor allegations) says Reuters reported in July 2022 that SMART, a Hyundai subsidiary in Luverne, Alabama, hired minors as young as 12 at a metal stamping plant. It says the US Department of Labor fined the supplier SL Alabama $30,076 on 29 September 2022, that neither labor department accused Hyundai or Kia of wrongdoing, and that on 24 February 2023 Hyundai's CEO Jae Hoon Chang said Hyundai would divest its controlling stake in SMART.
Hyundai Motor sponsored the Hyundai Motor Series from 2014 to February 2024; the report concerns its subsidiary SMART.
details.bottom_line: The museum is a state institution under the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, with a 12 billion won, ten-year Hyundai Motor sponsorship that ended in February 2024 and LG Electronics as title sponsor of a media art series from 2025. The weak points are the 2015 petitions against the director's appointment, the 2014 dismissal and 2023 resignation of directors, and the Unverified 2013 report on the opening show.

name: The War Memorial of Korea
funding: The Korea War Memorial Organization, a state-affiliated agency, runs the memorial; the Korea Times article read did not say how it is funded.
watch: A state-affiliated agency's war museum in Yongsan; in June 2026 it removed a poster and a Dandong memorial hall stop that gave China's account of the Korean War, and the Defense Ministry opened an inspection on 15 June 2026.
records_note: The pages read did not show published accounts.

overview: The war museum run by the Korea War Memorial Organization in Seoul (Korea Times, 9 June 2026).
The pages read did not state the opening year.
What is there: the pages read described education programmes on the 1950-53 war, not the collection.
Archive: the pages read did not mention an archive.
details.funding_verdict: War Memorial of Korea: state-affiliated agency, funding not stated in the pages read
funding: The Korea Times (9 June 2026) calls the organization a state-affiliated agency and does not say how it is funded.
The Defense Ministry's inspection of the agency was announced on 15 June 2026 (Korea JoongAng Daily).

red_flags.heading: Governance
points: On 9 June 2026 the Korea Times reported criticism of a poster for an elementary school programme titled The Korean War: Different Interpretations, which set South Korea's term next to China's account of resisting U.S. aggression. An agency official said the aim was critical analysis of China's claim, acknowledged the materials could be misunderstood, removed the poster and said the programme would proceed (Korea Times, 9 June 2026).

On 15 June 2026 the Defense Ministry announced an inspection after a Dandong memorial hall promoting China's account was added to a teacher training itinerary. Spokesperson Chung Binna called the itinerary a grave error; Defense Minister Ahn Gyu-back ordered a thorough investigation. The hall was removed from the itinerary and no findings were reported (Korea JoongAng Daily, 15 June 2026).

details.bottom_line: The pages read do not say who pays beyond calling the agency state-affiliated. The June 2026 row is about programme content and ministry oversight; the inspection had no reported result.

name: Bulegoa z/b
funding: Basque Government, Diputación Foral de Bizkaia, Bilbao City Council, the Creative Europe Programme of the EU and the Ministry of Culture and Sports support it.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
highlight: An office for art and knowledge in the Solokoetxe district of Bilbao that organises seminars, screenings, performances and talks.

overview: Independent "office for art and knowledge" at Solokoetxe 8 bajo, in the Solokoetxe district of Bilbao.

Started in 2010. The founding team included Isabel de Naverán, who worked with it until 2018. Current core members are Beatriz Cavia, Miren Jaio and Leire Vergara, with a board of advisers (stated by the space).
Full name: "Bulegoa zenbaki barik", shortened to Bulegoa z/b.

Works on critical pedagogy, situated knowledge, collaborative methods, feminism and decolonial perspectives, through seminars, screenings, performances, talks and artistic projects (stated by the space).
Programme lines on the site include Cine_ilegal, a film series (session 125 is listed for 12 November 2026), Formas de conocimiento informe, Producciones de una pared and open-call residencies.
Partner of the Dutch Art Institute from 2017 to 2025. Contributed to eight COOP study groups in the "Curating Positions" series, one per academic year (Dutch Art Institute).
details.funding_verdict: Bulegoa z/b: public: Basque Government, Bizkaia Provincial Council, Bilbao City Council, Spain's Ministry of Culture and Sports, and the EU's Creative Europe programme
funding: The space's own pages list "With the support of" the Basque Government (Eusko Jaurlaritza), the Diputación Foral de Bizkaia, Bilbao City Council, the Creative Europe Programme of the European Union and the Ministry of Culture and Sports, without years or amounts.
A 2020 post on the space's site says it was given the support of the Foundation for Arts Initiatives for a new project running from 2020 to 2023 (stated by the space).
details.bottom_line: The money behind the space is public culture funding from Basque, provincial, city, Spanish and EU bodies, plus one foundation's support for a 2020 to 2023 project. A 2026 article in Arte, Individuo y Sociedad by Irantzu Sanzo-San Martín and Concepción Elorza-Ibáñez de Gauna chooses the space as a case study of independent Bilbao initiatives that respond to the gentrification that followed the "Guggenheim effect"; its abstract says the space criticises the cultural, artistic and academic system.

name: Casa Bloc Museum-Apartment
funding: Barcelona's Institut de Cultura, through the Museu del Disseny, and the Generalitat's Institut Català del Sòl commissioned the apartment. Disseny Hub runs visits; the Generalitat owns the building.
watch: Dwelling 1/11, a flat in the Casa Bloc social-housing block, open for guided visits since February 2012. Tickets EUR 5, Saturdays.
records_note: It sits inside the city's Museu del Disseny.
affiliations_note: Visits run by Disseny Hub Barcelona, part of Barcelona City Council, with the Museu del Disseny and the Institut de Cultura; building owned by the Generalitat de Catalunya. Iconic Houses member, with a page on iconichouses.org that links to the Disseny Hub visit listing.

overview: Dwelling 1/11, a 60 m² duplex in block 2 of the Casa Bloc social-housing complex in Sant Andreu, at Almirall Pròixida on the corner with Passeig de Torras i Bages (Catalan Wikipedia; Disseny Hub page).

The republican Generalitat's Institut Contra l'Atur Forçós commissioned Casa Bloc in 1932. The GATCPAC architects Josep Lluís Sert, Josep Torres Clavé and Joan Baptista Subirana designed it, and Francesc Macià laid the first stone in March 1933 (Catalan Wikipedia).

The complex is five seven-storey blocks in an inverted "S". Work stopped in the civil war and the Franco regime finished it for military families. The Diputació de Barcelona held it after the war and it returned to the Generalitat after democracy. It became a Bé Cultural d'Interès Nacional in 1992, and in 1997 INCASÒL, the Diputació and the Ajuntament signed a rehabilitation agreement (Catalan Wikipedia).

The Institut de Cultura de Barcelona, through the Museu del Disseny (then DHUB), and INCASÒL commissioned the apartment's restoration by Marta Montmany, Rossend Casanova and Víctor and Marc Seguí. It opened to guided visits in February 2012 (Catalan Wikipedia).

Rossend Casanova calls it a restored original, not a recreation. It holds a purpose-made sideboard, two wardrobes, two bedside tables and a bed, the double bedroom's pieces made from instructions published in the magazine A.C. (Docomomo Journal 47, 2012).

Visiting: guided tours on Saturdays at 11:00, 90 minutes, in Catalan, and in Spanish on the last Saturday of the month. EUR 5 per person, EUR 75 for a group of up to 15. Closed all of August, the first two weekends of September, 1 January, 1 May, 24 June, 25 and 28 December. Only the ground floor of the duplex is wheelchair accessible (Disseny Hub page).
details.funding_verdict: Casa Bloc Museum-Apartment: public: Barcelona City Council and the Generalitat's INCASÒL
funding: The Institut de Cultura de Barcelona and INCASÒL commissioned the restoration. Disseny Hub Barcelona runs the visits, and its page says INCASÒL supports the tour (Disseny Hub page; Catalan Wikipedia).

INCASÒL, the Generalitat's land institute, owns the building and commissioned its rehabilitation by the architects Víctor and Marc Seguí, including the 2008 demolition of the "Bloc fantasma" (Docomomo Journal; Catalan Wikipedia).

press.overall: The Docomomo Journal piece on the apartment is by Rossend Casanova, who writes of the apartment's opening as "we", and is not criticism.

details.bottom_line: Barcelona's city council and the Generalitat's land institute commissioned the apartment, Disseny Hub Barcelona runs the visits, and no flagged funder appears. The weak points are that no budget, restoration cost or visitor figure is published and that access is one Saturday tour a week, in Catalan, with the upper floor not wheelchair accessible. Watch the conservation master plan announced in 2022.

name: Casa de la Arquitectura
funding: The state museum is attached to the Ministerio de Vivienda y Agenda Urbana (Wikipedia, The Objective).
watch: Magmacultura cut two mediators' hours from 90% to 60% in February 2026, then withdrew the change and agreed to pay the wage difference.

overview: National architecture museum at La Arquería de Nuevos Ministerios, Paseo de la Castellana 67, Madrid.

Opened on 18 December 2023. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez spoke at the opening and said the opening formally meets one of the mandates of the Ley de Calidad de la Arquitectura (La Moncloa). Earlier the Museo Nacional de Arquitectura y Urbanismo, established on 29 December 2006 (Wikipedia).
Ley 9/2022 on the Quality of Architecture, approved on 14 June 2022, gave it the name Casa de la Arquitectura (Wikipedia). A royal decree of December 2023 created and regulates it (The Objective).

The building has space for a permanent collection and temporary exhibitions. A board of trustees, chaired by the museum director, includes the Housing and Culture ministries and architects' associations (Wikipedia).
Open Tuesday to Saturday 11:00 to 20:00, Sundays and holidays 11:00 to 15:00. Exhibitions, guided tours and workshops are free.
details.funding_verdict: Casa de la Arquitectura: public: Spain's Ministry of Housing and Urban Agenda
funding: In December 2025 the ministry put out to tender the design of the museum's extension for 1,722,974.15 euros including VAT, covering new galleries, a library, conservation areas and a plan for the Nuevos Ministerios outdoor spaces (Forbes España).
The website footer shows the logos of the Gobierno de España and Fundación Arquia; no reporting found of what Fundación Arquia pays for.

red_flags.heading: Labour dispute with contractor staff
points: Magmacultura SL took over the cultural mediation service in November 2025; in early February it told staff that conditions would change from 21 February, which the union said could cut hours by up to 24 a month (SUT, the union that organised the strike).
SUT called an indefinite strike from 5 March, joined by the information staff of Sedena SL; at the mediation on 4 March the Ministry of Housing did not appear (SUT).
The museum was closed for eight days; Magmacultura then revoked the change and agreed to pay the wage differences (SUT).

press.overall: Coverage found, such as Arquitectura Viva's December 2023 opening report, is descriptive.

details.bottom_line: The museum is a state body paid for by the Ministry of Housing, with no private funder named beyond a Fundación Arquia logo. The weak points are a contractor pay dispute in 2026 that closed the museum for eight days, and a .gob.es address that now serves an unrelated crypto app. Worth watching: the 1.7 million euro extension and who holds the old domain.

name: Centre d'Art la Panera
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.

overview: Public contemporary art centre at Plaça de la Panera 2, Lleida, in a medieval building. It describes itself as a platform for producing and spreading contemporary visual arts, with research, education and public programmes, and projects in schools, health centres and community services.

The centre's own page says it was inaugurated in 2003, taking up the Biennal d'Art Leandre Cristòfol that the city of Lleida began in 1997, and that the centre's collection grew from the biennial. English Wikipedia gives 1997 as the year the centre opened, with the introduction of the biennial.
Christian Alonso won the competition for its direction in July 2022 (Bonart) and has directed it since then (Wikipedia).

Building: known as the Almodí, built between the 12th and 13th centuries as the city's trading hall for grain, oil and grapes. 21 medieval stone columns, each 5.70 metres high, survive. In 1606 the cathedral canons bought it and added a floor, giving it the name La Panera dels Canonges. After the 1835 Desamortització it passed to the Paeria (city council), which ceded it to the army. It became a cavalry barracks in 1860 and later a national police barracks until the late 1980s, when it returned to the Paeria and was chosen as the site for an art centre.

Programme: exhibitions on two floors, a children's space (MiniPanera), a documentation centre with a fund of special editions and artists' books, a publishing programme and a typography residency, school and secondary-school artist residencies, and public programmes on art and technology, functional diversity and mental health.
Visiting: open Tuesday to Saturday 10:00 to 14:00 and 17:00 to 19:00, Sundays and public holidays 11:00 to 14:00, closed Mondays.
details.funding_verdict: Centre d'Art La Panera: public, by the centre's own account: Ajuntament de Lleida and the Generalitat de Catalunya
funding: Stated by the centre: it is a public facility, the result of cooperation between the Ajuntament de Lleida and the Department of Culture of the Generalitat de Catalunya.

It belongs to the Network of Territorial Visual Arts Centres of Catalonia, part of the Generalitat's public visual arts system, with ACVic, Bòlit (Girona), Centre d'Art Tarragona, Tecla Sala (L'Hospitalet), Fabra i Coats (Barcelona), Mataró Art Contemporani and Lo Pati (Amposta). The network's centres are municipally owned and promoted by the Generalitat.
details.bottom_line: The centre calls itself a public facility created through cooperation between the Ajuntament de Lleida and the Department of Culture of the Generalitat de Catalunya, within the Generalitat's network of territorial visual arts centres. The building returned to the Paeria (city council) in the late 1980s.
